text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **

Grazier and Tasmanian pioneer, EDWARD CURR, was born in 1798. He was known for his argumentative nature and he contested on principle almost every decision made by the government, and ended-up in politics!

Australian poet, DOROTHEA MACKELLAR, was born in 1853. She was home educated by her wealthy Sydney family, and wrote several novels including "Outlaw's Luck". When she was 19, DOROTHEA wrote a poem called "Core of My Heart", which became better known as the classic "My Country."
English aviator, AMY JOHNSON, who flew from London to Australia in 1930 and crashed in Brisbane, was born in 1903. She broke many solo flight records, and died in 1941 as a wartime ferry pilot.

American actress, OLIVIA DE HAVILLAND, was born in 1916. She won Oscars for "The Heiress" and "To Each His Own". American singer, songwriter and actress, DEBORAH HARRY, was born in 1945. She started a folk-rock band in the sixties, worked as a playboy bunny and barmaid, and formed the band 'Angel and the Snakes' in 1974. A year later the band became 'Blondie' and went on to have a string of hits. These included "Heart Of Glass"(1979), "Call Me" (1980) and "The Tide Is High" (1980).

"The Voice", JOHN FARNHAM, was born in 1949 in England. He came to Australia in 1959 and became one of the country's best-liked and most respected singers. When he was 18 he made his first single "Sadie- The Cleaning Lady", which reached number one on the Australian charts. He spent four years in the early eighties as leadsinger of the 'Little River Band' before resuming his solo career. His more recent hits include "You're The Voice" and "Age Of Reason."
Aboriginal actor DAVID GULPILIL was born in Arnhem Land in 1953. After winning four Eisteddfod awards for dancing, he made his first film in 1971 called "Walkabout".
The Princess of Wales, LADY DIANA SPENCER, was born in 1961. She is descended from CHARLES II. She married the PRINCE OF WALES on July the 29th, 1981.
American athlete, CARL LEWIS, was also born in 1961. LEWIS won three gold medals in the Los Angeles Olympic Games in 1984.
** EVENTS **
1097 : The Crusaders defeated the Turks at Dorylaeum in
the First Crusade.
1824 : Governor of New South Wales LACHLAN MACQUARIE died

at the age of 62. He had returned to London in 1822 after serving as governor for 12 years. Governor MACQUARIE has been remembered as a visionary, who built the free charity school at Parramatta, and in 1814 established the Native Institution to
educate young Aborigines. He introduced a system of coins to the colony and encouraged the creation of the Bank of New South Wales.
1847 : The first adhesive stamps went on sale in the
United States.
1858 : British scientist CHARLES DARWIN presented his
controversial theory of evolution in London. DARWIN based much of his work on observations while serving as a naturalist on HMS Beagle in South America and the Galapagos Islands. His published

works "Origin of the Species" explained evolutionary processes through natural and sexual selection. His views aroused bitter controversy because they contradicted the literal interpretation of the Book of Genesis in the Bible.
1860 : CHARLES GOODYEAR, U.S. inventor of the vulcanised
rubber process, died; infringements of his copyright left him $200,000 in debt.
1863 : General ROBERT E. LEE with Confederate troops
launched an attack, beginning the battle of Gettysburg in the U.S. civil war.
1866 : Umpires were used for the first time in Australian

Rules Football, in a game between Carlton and Melbourne. However, umpires didn't became a permanent fixture until 1872. Prior to this, the captains of each team would determine the penalties and free kicks.
1867 : The Dominion of Canada was established under the
British North America Act.
1898 : Britain acquired a 99-year lease to the New

Territories on mainland China. Britain had acquired Hong Kong island and the Kowloon Peninsula after the two Opium wars. The lease on the New Territories expired today and Britain handed back sovereignty to the Chinese government.
1907 : The world's first air force was established with
the formation of the Aeronautical Division of the Office of the Chief Signal Officer of the U.S. army.
1916 : The distinctively shaped Coca-Cola bottle was

officially launched. The drink, made from coca leaves and flavoured with cola nuts, was already on sale in every American State. It was invented in 1886, and by 1987 was sold in 155 countries. The sweetened, carbonated drink also contains caramel and caffeine.
1916 : The battle of the Somme began with heavy

casualties. The World War I offensive continued until November 1916, with severe losses on both sides. The Allies lost more than 600,000 men and advanced 32 km. It was the first battle involving tanks.
1929 : Spinach-munching cartoon character POPEYE made his
first appearance in the United States.
1940 : German troops landed on the Channel Island of
Jersey.
1941 : The first television commercial was broadcast on
channel WNBT in New York. The commercial was advertising a Bulova clock.
1944 : The Bretton Woods Conference began under the
auspices of the U.N. to formulate post-war international monetary policy.
1946 : The U.S. tested its atomic bomb over the Bikini
Atoll in the Pacific.
1963 : The Queen installed Australian Prime Minister
ROBERT MENZIES as a Knight of the Thistle.
1969 : PRINCE CHARLES, heir to the British throne, was
invested as the Prince of Wales by his mother, QUEEN ELIZABETH II. When PRINCE CHARLES becomes King the title will cease, until he bestows it on his son.
1974 : JUAN PERON, Argentine president (1946-55) and founder of the Peronista movement, died.
1974 : In Australia, federal cabinet accepted the
WOODWARD report that recommended all Northern Territory reserves and missions should be handed over to Aborigines.
1984 : Naples football club paid 1.85 million dollars for
Argentinian footballer DIEGO MARADONA.
1989 : The break-up of the Soviet Union was foreshadowed.

Soviet President GORBACHEV announced on television broadcast throughout the USSR that he would not tolerate separatism. The warning came after a groundswell of nationalist sentiment among a number of Soviet republics. Independence movements were well underway in the Baltic states.
1994 : Argentine soccer legend DIEGO MARADONA was kicked
out of the national team after testing positive to drugs at the World Cup in the United States.
1996 : The Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine
said it was suspending its membership in the PLO and urged other groups to work to cancel the PLO-Israeli peace deals.
